title: English Vlog 🇺🇸 | My Fear of Failure (Listening & Shadowing Practice)
channel: Speak English with Bo's Slow English

lines.text: Hello everyone. My name is Bo and this
is Bo's Slow English. Lately, I've been
thinking about anxiety and fear. Whether
I was always anxious or if it slowly
developed over time. I think many people
assume that anxiety means you're always
weak or you're always scared. Today, I
want to talk about when I first remember
feeling anxious and how it showed up
throughout different parts of my life.
And I want to talk about how my
relationship with anxiety has changed as
I've gotten older. After you watch this
video, let me know in the comments if
any of this resonated with you or if you
relate to it. Please like, subscribe,
and share this video with your friends.
And please check out my new YouTube
channel. It's for kids, families, and
super beginner English learners. When I
think about anxiety, I don't think I was
born anxious. In fact, one of my first
memories is actually feeling confident.
The first year I played soccer, I was
good.
I remember kicking the ball really hard.
Apparently, hard enough that referees
checked my cleats because they thought
maybe I had metal in them.
I was proud of myself.
And then, something changed.
I skipped sixth grade soccer. And when I
returned in seventh grade, I remember
feeling afraid.
Not only afraid of getting hit by the
ball, but afraid of failing, afraid of
disappointing my team,
afraid of not doing a good job.
I remember when the ball came toward me,
I would overthink.
And when you overthink,
sometimes your body freezes.
Your mind becomes louder than your
instincts.
I think that may have been one of the
first times I noticed anxiety.
I just didn't have the words for it.
Around that same time, I tried
snowboarding.
I took a group lesson.
And instead of enjoying it, I compared
myself to everyone else.
Who was better?
Who learned faster?
Who looked confident? And instead of
enjoying it, I compared myself to
everyone else.
I was so preoccupied with who was better
than me, who learned faster than me, who
looked more confident than me.
I was afraid of falling.
I was afraid of getting hurt.
And maybe more than that, I was afraid
of failing once [clears throat] again.
That's interesting to think about now.
Because fear of failure followed me for
a long time.
Nowadays, when I hear negative thoughts
in my head, I can separate them more.
There's a concept called your inner
child.
Your inner child is basically younger
versions of yourself.
Experiences,
fears, or beliefs you carry into
childhood.
Sometimes I hear a voice that says,
"You can't do it."
But now I know that voice isn't always
logical.
Sometimes it's fear,
and sometimes it's old patterns.
And sometimes it's simply a younger
version of me trying to protect me.
My anxiety was probably worse again in
my 20s.
I moved to Los Angeles when I was around
20 years old.
I drove across the country.
I barely knew anyone.
I didn't have everything planned.
Normally, people think planning reduces
stress.
I actually tend to wing things.
Winging it means doing something without
fully planning,
which sounds strange because people
often think I'm very organized.
But big life decisions,
I sometimes jump.
I moved to LA because I wanted change.
I wanted growth,
and I was excited.
But excitement and anxiety can exist
together.
I think people forget that.
LA felt lonely sometimes. I met people
who I eventually realized were not
helping me become the person I wanted to
be.
Not terrible people,
just negative,
self-deprecating,
unmotivated,
and I learned something difficult.
Sometimes protecting your peace means
changing who you spend time with.
That can be lonely, especially in a huge
city.
People today sometimes think I'm
confident. Clients probably see me as
calm, capable,
organized.
But anxiety doesn't always look obvious.
When I worked in luxury salons,
there was pressure.
People trust you with their appearance,
their confidence.
Now working in clinics, there's
pressure, too.
People trust you with their face,
their emotions,
their health.
And when you care deeply about doing
well,
anxiety can hide underneath
responsibility.
For me,
anxiety often feels physical.
Shallow breathing, overthinking,
feeling overwhelmed.
Almost like my body is speeding up
before my mind catches up.
I think one reason I manage anxiety
better now is because I respect my body
more.
I try to eat when I'm hungry.
I take breaks.
I pause.
I used to ignore those things.
Working in salons taught me to push
through lunch,
push through exhaustion,
push through stress.
But pushing forever isn't sustainable.
I also think losing friends young
changed me.
It made me realize time matters.
Life is shorter than we expect.
Because of that, I try harder to do
things I enjoy.
And if something consistently takes away
my peace,
I think seriously about changing
direction.
The interesting thing is I don't think
anxiety made me weaker.
I think in some ways it made me braver.
Because when you spend years feeling
afraid and still keep trying new things,
moving cities,
changing careers,
building businesses,
showing up online,
you realize courage is not the absence
of fear.
Sometimes courage is doing things while
fear is sitting beside you.
If I could talk to younger me standing
on the soccer field, I think I'd say,
"You can do it and I'm here for you."
I still hear that fearful voice
sometimes. I just don't believe
everything it says anymore and I think
that's growth. I would love to know in
the comments,
did you learn any new vocabulary words
from this video? If you relate to my
story, please let me know. I'll see you
at the next story time.
Bye.
